## Background

Today we will explore some core machine learning methods that are very popular in bioinformatics. These include **clustering** and **dimensionallity reduction**. 

## K-means

The main function in "base R" for K-means clustering is called `kmeans()`

Before we go too deep let's make up some "simple" data that we can cluster and know if we are getting good results or not. To do this we can use the `rnorm()` function:

```{r}
rnorm(10)
```

```{r}
hist(rnorm(100000))
```

Give me 30 points centered at -3 and a second set with a mean of +3 

```{r}
tmp <- c( rnorm(30, mean = -3), rnorm(30, mean = +3) )

x <- cbind(x = tmp, y = rev(tmp))
x
```

```{r}
rev( letters[1:5] )
```

```{r}
plot(x)
```

Now try `kmeans()` on this input data `x`

```{r}
k <- kmeans(x, centers = 2)
k
```

To get the results we can use `k$size` etc. to get each component result:

> Q. How many points are in each cluster?

```{r}
k$size
```

> Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster membership?

```{r}
k$cluster
```


> Q. What "component" of your results object details cluster centers?

```{r}
k$centers
```

> Q. Make a results figure of our data with points colored by cluster along with cluster centers?

```{r}
plot(x, col = k$cluster)
points(k$centers, col = "blue", pch = 15)

```

> Q. Run kmeans again and cluster into 4 clusters producing a results figure with points colored by cluster and showing the cluster centers

```{r}
knew <- kmeans(x, centers = 4)
knew
```

```{r}
knew$cluster
```

```{r}
plot(x, col = knew$cluster)
points(knew$centers, col = "blue", pch = 15)
```

> **N.B.** You need to tell K-means the number of clusters (i.e. set `centers=2`)!!

One approach is to try different values for `centers` and then pick the best one:

```{r}
ans <- NULL

for(i in 1:10){
  #cat(i, "\n")
  km <- kmeans(x, centers = i)
  ans <- c(ans, km$tot.withinss)
}
```

```{r}
plot(ans, typ = "o",
     xlab = "Number of clusters",
     ylab = "Total sum of Squares Distance")
```


## Hierarchical Clustering

The main function in "base" R for Hierarchical Clustering is called `hclust()`

This function does not take your "raw" data for clustering. You must first build a "distance matrix" from your data and pass this as input for `hclust()`.

```{r}
d <- dist(x)
hc <- hclust(d)
hc
```

```{r}
plot(hc)
abline(h = 8, col = "red")
```

Once we have our `hclust` object (our "tree" or "cluster dendrogram") we can "cut" the tree to reveal the clustering pattern.

```{r}
cutree(hc, h = 8)
```

You can use either `h=` or `k=` arguments to `cutree()`

```{r}
cutree(hc, k = 4)
```

> Q. Make a plot of input data `x` with your clusters from `hclust()` (i.e colored by cluster membership from cutting the tree)?

```{r}
cut <- cutree(hc, k = 8)
plot(x, col = cut)
```
## Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

PCA is a dimensionality reduction method that is popular for revealing patterns in complex datasets.

### Analysis of UK food data

Let's look at some data on eating habits of folks from the UK to see if there are patterns and trends that have some regions being distinct from others.

### Data import

The data is made available in CSV format so we can use `read.csv()`:

```{r}
x <- read.csv("https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods", row.names = 1)
x
```

> Q1. How many rows and columns are in your new data frame named x? What R functions could you use to answer these questions?

You can use the R functions nrow() to return the row number, ncol() to return the column number, and then dim() returns both.
There are 17 rows and 4 columns in the data frame.

```{r}
nrow(x)
ncol(x)
dim(x)
```

> Q2. Which approach to solving the `row-names problem` mentioned above do you prefer and why? Is one approach more robust than another under certain circumstances?

This method doesn't work because it deletes the first column every time you rerun the code
```{r}
rownames(x) <- x[,1]
x <- x[,-1]
head(x)
dim(x)
```

This approach below is something that is preferred because it ensures that when you rerun the code it does not delete the column. This is more robust and safer when working in situations where you need to rerun the code multiple times. 
```{r}
x <- read.csv("https://tinyurl.com/UK-foods", row.names = 1)
head(x)
```

Some plots:

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=T, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```

> Q3. Changing what optional argument in the above barplot() function results in the following plot?

Changing beside to False instead of True makes a stacked bar plot. 

```{r}
barplot(as.matrix(x), beside=F, col=rainbow(nrow(x)))
```


```{r}
library(tidyr)
x_long <- x |>
  tibble::rownames_to_column("Food") |>
  pivot_longer(cols = -Food,
               names_to = "Country",
               values_to = "Consumption")
head(x_long)
```
Initial plot:
```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  theme_bw()
```

> Q4. Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?

You can change "dodge" to "stack" in position to create a stacked barplot figure.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(x_long) +
  aes(x = Country, y = Consumption, fill = Food) +
  geom_col(position = "stack") +
  theme_bw()
```


### Pairs plots and heatmaps

One plot that can be useful for relatively small datasets is a `pairs()` plot:Changing what optional argument in the above ggplot() code results in a stacked barplot figure?

```{r}
pairs(x, col=rainbow(nrow(x)), pch=16)
```

> Q5. We can use the pairs() function to generate all pairwise plots for our countries. Can you make sense of the following code and resulting figure? What does it mean if a given point lies on the diagonal for a given plot?

The pairs() function in the code above creates grids of scatterplots to compare the countries vs countries. It allows us to see whether the 2 have similar food consumptions through patterns. If the point lies on the diagonal, this means both countries consume the same amount of food for that specific food item.

```{r}
library(pheatmap)

pheatmap( as.matrix(x) )
```

> Q6. Based on the pairs and heatmap figures, which countries cluster together and what does this suggest about their food consumption patterns? Can you easily tell what the main differences between N. Ireland and the other countries of the UK in terms of this data-set?

England, Wales, and Scotland cluster together and N. Ireland is grouped further away. This suggests N. Ireland food consumption patterns differ from the rest. 
The main differences are from the data points being further away from the diagonal lines on the pairs() plot. I cannot tell fairly easily but the data set broadly reveals that N. Ireland consumes more Fresh Potatoes and Soft Drinks but less Fresh Fruit and Alcoholic Drinks compared to the other 3. 


> **Key-point**: Even relatively small datasets can prove challenging to interpret 

Given that it is quite difficult to make sense of even this relatively small data set. Hopefully, we can clearly see that a powerful analytical method is absolutely necessary if we wish to observe trends and patterns in larger datasets.

## PCA to the rescue!

The main function in "base" R for PCA is called `prcomp()`: 

This function will require the transpose of our dataset

```{r}
pca <- prcomp (t(x))
```

We can see how well or PCA results are doing in terms of *variance captured* from the original data in each PC.

```{r}
summary(pca)
```
I can see what is in my `pca` result object by:
```{r}
attributes(pca)
```
Of these `pca$x` is our main result. We can use it to make a results figure often called a PCA plot (or score-plot).

```{r}
pca$x
```

> Q7. Complete the code below to generate a plot of PC1 and PC2. The second line adds text labels over the data points.

Completed code with blanks filled:
```{r}
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)

ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = rownames(pca$x)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```

> Q8. Customize your plot so that the colors of the country names match the colors in our UK and Ireland map and table at start of this document.

```{r}
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(pca$x, aes(PC1, PC2)) + 
  geom_point(col = c("orange", "red", "blue", "darkgreen"))
  
```

Remade the graph:
```{r}
df <- as.data.frame(pca$x)
df$Country <- rownames(df)
colors <- c("England" = "orange", "Scotland" = "blue", "Wales" = "red", "N.Ireland" = "darkgreen")

ggplot(pca$x) +
  aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, label = rownames(pca$x), color =  rownames(pca$x)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  geom_text(vjust = -0.5) +
  scale_color_manual(values = colors) +
  xlim(-270, 500) +
  xlab("PC1") +
  ylab("PC2") +
  theme_bw()
```


A "loadings plot" can show us how the original dimensions/variables contribute to our new PC axis. This is detailed in the `pca$rotation` component of our result object:

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(PC1, rownames(pca$rotation)) +
  geom_col()
```

## Digging deeper (variable loadings)

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(x = PC1, 
      y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC1)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC1 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```

> Q9. Generate a similar `loadings plot` for PC2. What two food groups feature prominantely and what does PC2 mainly tell us about?

In the PC1 plot, the fresh potatoes and soft drinks are both at the top but now in the PC2 plot, the soft drinks are at the top but the fresh potatoes are at the bottom.
The two groups feature prominently in PC2 are fresh potatoes and soft drinks. It mainly tells us the 2nd largest source of variance in data, showing the second most defining difference between the countries. 

```{r}
ggplot(pca$rotation) +
  aes(x = PC2, y = reorder(rownames(pca$rotation), PC2)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  xlab("PC2 Loading Score") +
  ylab("") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9))
```
